newsitem.title: USA: U.S Jan trade gap balloons, dents Q1 GDP estimates.
newsitem.headline: U.S Jan trade gap balloons, dents Q1 GDP estimates.

text.p: A sharp rise in imports and a solid decline in exports spurred a sizable widening of the U.S. trade deficit in January, putting a dent in many economists' forecasts for first quarter U.S. economic growth.

"People had been assuming there wouldn't be much of a subtraction from net exports in the first quarter," said John Rothfield, international economist at Nationsbanc in Chicago. "But now there is going to be a significant downward revision to first quarter GDP."

The Commerce Department reported on Thursday that the overall U.S. trade deficit in goods and services for January ballooned 21.1 percent to $12.71 billion in January, its highest level in nearly a decade.
This compared to Wall Street forecasts for a $10.7 billion gap and a revised December shortfall of $10.49 billion.

Exports declined 0.6 percent in January while imports rose at a heady 2.2 percent clip, due to higher oil prices and record imports of industrial supplies and materials, capital goods as well as autos and automobile parts.
"It's indicative of the strength of the economy and possibly the stronger dollar which is making imports relatively cheap and more attractive," said Chris Iggo, chief economist at BZW Securities.
Based on the retreat in exports, however, Iggo said his estimates for first quarter gross domestic product would be revised down from 4.0 percent to roughly 3.5 percent.
"It's only one month's number and we don't know what February and March are going to be like but that would be our estimate at the moment," he noted.
The dollar appreciated by roughly 4.7 percent against the yen and by 6.3 percent against the mark during January.
A reassuring aspect of the report, economists said, was the relative stability seen in the bilateral trade deficit with Japan.
The politically sensitive U.S. gap with Japan edged higher by 0.7 percent to $4.29 billion in January but failed to confirm the market's worst fears.
Recent Japanese trade numbers had shown substantial gains in its surplus with the U.S. for both January and February.
"The deficits with Japan and Western Europe weren't such a bad thing," said David Sloan, economist at I.D.E.A. Inc. "It seems to me the biggest problems are with China and Mexico."

The U.S. shortfall with China surged again in January by 40.8 percent, totaling $3.72 billion. Economists said these numbers could do further damage to already tense trade relations between the two countries.
The trade gap with key trading partner Mexico soared by 92.4 percent in January, but analysts said this was offset somewhat by improvement in the U.S. deficit with its other NAFTA neighbor Canada.

Economists and Commerce Department officials shied away from attributing the widening deficit to the strong dollar, saying growth differentials between the U.S. and its trading partners were probably the chief culprit.
"It's hard to separate (the impact of the dollar) from other factors operating in the deficit this time," said U.S. Commerce Undersecretary Everett Ehrlich.
"We've seen the deficit increase in the last several months and that's coincident with some changes in exchange rates, but it's also coincident with changes in growth differentials."

The impact of today's trade figures on the dollar was mixed. Some traders seized on the strength of imports as a sign of strong growth and higher U.S. rates, while others worried about the impact of declining U.S. exports and potential tensions with Asian trading partners.
((--N.A. Treasury Desk 212-859-1673))
